newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to keep 98 govt spending rise below GDP.
newsitem.headline: France to keep 98 govt spending rise below GDP.

text.p: French government spending rises will be kept well below the pace of economic growth next year and help limit France's public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product for European monetary union, a finance ministry source said on Tuesday.
"Government spending will rise very significantly less than gross domestic product (GDP)," the source said.

"This result will be obtained through savings which will allow us to reach the target of three percent for all departments without increasing state levies. This is consistent with the government's will to take care of its debt problem," the source added.

The 1998 budget, crucial to the new Socialist-led government's plans for joining Europe's single currency, was being prepared in the context of stronger economic growth next year, but spending would in any case be strictly controlled, the source said.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin interrupted his summer holiday to put the finishing touches last Friday to the spending side of the budget and will shortly return to Paris again to work on the rest of the package.

Pending the outcome of those deliberations, which will focus on the revenue side, the only official growth forecast for 1998 is one made by the previous centre-right government and predicts growth in GDP of 2.8 percent.
Prior to Tuesday's limited insight into Jospin's work on the spending side, the government had maintained a veil of silence.
But various newspaper comments have suggested the defence ministry's budget could be hit once again, after a decision in July to knock two billion francs ($318.6 million) off its initial 1997 budget.
Business daily La Tribune cited anonymous sources on Tuesday as saying the defence budget could be cut to 82 or 83 billion francs in 1998 from an already reduced 1997 allocation of 84.9 billion.
The finance ministry source reiterated that the government's priorities were employment, education, research and justice.

Employment Minister Martine Aubry, who is second-in-command to Jospin at the head of a beefed-up employment ministry, said last Friday that the talks concerning her share of the 1998 budget had "gone well".

Aubry is due to present legislation in September to back up the government's promise to create 350,000 jobs for the young in the public sector and the cost of funding 100,000 of those jobs next year has been put at 10 billion francs.

Jospin and other leading government members have said the jobs plan will not require new funds and Aubry is expected to generate much of the money needed by scaling back on other job subsidies which are seen as less efficient.
The finance bill is due to be completed and presented for cabinet approval on September 24.

Finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said when unveiling an audit of French state finances in July that the public deficit was heading for betweem 3.5 and 3.7 percent of GDP this year and he presented a 32-billion-franc package of corporate taxes and other savings to bring it down by 0.4 percentage points.

He has said France could well miss the three percent deficit target but that it will get there in 1998 and it is the trend that counts when interpreting the Maastricht treaty's goal of a three percent deficit to join monetary union in 1999.
What counts now is the growth prediction and tax revenue forecasts the government comes up with as well as other non-fiscal revenues.

Financial daily L'Agefi said on Tuesday that the government had decided to tap about 30 billion francs ($4.8 billion) from state-owned utility Electricite de France-Gaz de France's accounts to help plug the hole in next year's budget.

The one-time payment would come from money EdF-GdF has already provisioned for the construction of a Rhine-Rhone canal, the paper said without naming any sources. Jospin's government had cancelled the canal project for environmental reasons.
The 30 billion francs would single-handedly cut about 0.3 percent of GDP from the central government deficit and make it much easier for France to respect the EMU deficit criterion.
French governments routinely tap state-owned companies such as state bank Caisse des Depots for so-called non-fiscal budgetary receipts.

But the former government's use of a 37-billion-franc France Telecom payment in the 1997 accounts, which cut 0.45 percent off the deficit, was seen as exceptionally big -- requiring another big transfer this year to fill the gap.
